title: Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a robot hand that autonomously adjusts and regrasps objects within its fingers, uses ordinary hand tools, and manipulates deformable objects such as cloth or bags, including objects unfamiliar from training. It would perform these operations at human-comparable speed and reliability over sustained sessions. The target combines these abilities in one system; a successful demonstration of one specialized manipulation skill would establish only part of the capability.

In-hand manipulation means changing an object's position or orientation relative to the palm through coordinated finger movements and changing contacts. It includes releasing and restoring individual contacts while other fingers stabilize the object. This adds capabilities beyond grasping an object and moving the whole hand: the robot must manage intermittent contact, slipping and multiple points of support while preserving useful control.

Scope synthesis: ROB-02 concerns dependable manual skill. Transfer of one architecture across different robot hands would strengthen the result, but is an additional generalization target rather than a requirement for this concept. Neither broad occupational competence nor safe deployment alongside people follows automatically from dexterity.

significance.text: Reliable finger-level manipulation would substantially expand the operations available to robots in environments built around human hands. Parallel-jaw grippers have limitations when tasks require adjustment within the grasp, stabilization at several contact points or tool-like interactions. Overcoming these limitations would let robots maintain and alter a grasp as a task develops, extending the range of operations they can complete with ordinary objects.

Conditional impact synthesis: autonomous tool use, object adjustment and deformable handling could supply important manual capabilities for maintenance, trades, food preparation and garment work. Human-comparable reliability would matter as much as an impressive individual movement: repeated drops, frequent resets or slow recovery could make an otherwise capable hand impractical. The revolutionary consequence would be a broad expansion of dependable physical operations; complete jobs would additionally require perception, planning and application-specific knowledge.

The analogy to a human hand has practical limits. Matching selected manipulation tasks would not establish human versatility across all materials, tools or environments. Safe collaboration would require additional evidence about the complete robot and its deployment conditions. DeepMind's linked July 2026 safety report explicitly excludes evaluation of the underlying functional safety architecture, illustrating why reported manipulation progress and safety evaluations cannot alone establish readiness for work beside people.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied demonstrations is integrated autonomous control across unfamiliar rigid objects, ordinary tools and deformables, with sustained human-comparable performance. Existing hands and specialist policies demonstrate substantial skills, but the reviewed sources do not demonstrate this combined target. They also do not establish the stronger claim that no qualifying system exists anywhere.

A central engineering barrier is high-dimensional contact control. Many actuated joints must coordinate through contacts that appear, disappear, stick and slip. Small errors in object state, contact estimates or physical models can change what movement is possible and whether the object remains held. DexSuite identifies high-dimensional actuation, intermittent contacts and sensitivity to modeling errors as reasons dexterous hands are difficult to teleoperate, train and evaluate. Extending such control to changing object shapes adds another challenge to the proposed scope.

The challenge cannot be assigned solely to policy learning. Perception must provide sufficiently useful state information during contact, while the hand must have the physical range and actuation needed for the desired movement. Chuang and colleagues used motion capture for their state-based policies and reported that rotating a lightbulb with the palm facing down could become difficult at some poses, potentially reflecting hardware limitations as well as policy limitations. A hand that can form useful grasps does not necessarily support every required manipulation.

Generalization and sustained recovery remain separate hurdles from reaching an isolated goal. Per-object training does not demonstrate adaptation to unfamiliar objects, and repeated goal attempts with manual resets do not establish uninterrupted autonomous operation. A convincing advance must maintain useful performance through different wrist orientations and disturbances while accounting for drops, sticking and recovery. The reviewed LEAP-hand study explicitly treats reliability, safety and robustness as important alongside success rate.

current_state.text: The research identifies Aude Billard and Danica Kragic's “Trends and challenges in robot manipulation,” published in Science on June 21, 2019, as historical context for dexterity remaining an open problem. However, no article or structured-abstract artifact was retained for the supplied review. Its attributed wording could therefore not be checked, and it should not carry the evidentiary burden for the present assessment. This access limitation does not show that the attribution is false.

DexSuite, submitted to arXiv on October 27, 2026, reports an open-source simulation framework and benchmark, together with 4,700 successful simulated episodes collected through human teleoperation, scripted experts and learned policies. This is a reported simulation resource, not 4,700 demonstrations of autonomous real-world human-level dexterity. The mixture of episode-generation methods also means that successful dataset episodes should not be treated as a single learned policy's autonomous benchmark performance. The supplied review supports the release statement from the paper's text; it does not establish independent reproduction of the software or results.

In a separate arXiv report submitted October 27, 2026, Ian Chuang and colleagues evaluated in-hand manipulation on a LEAP hand. Their evaluation comprised 4,800 goal attempts across four configurations, four objects and six wrist orientations, with 13.3 hours of goal windows. These totals pool the configurations; they are not the denominator or operating duration of the single policy result associated with the headline 95.2% success rate.

The unfiltered state-policy configuration reached 95.2% of its 1,200 goals at the coarse tolerance of 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and 75.6% at the paper's more precise tolerance. Orientation scoring for the lightbulb and wineglass used axis tilt, which limits interpretation of the angular tolerance as full orientation matching. Goals were unseen, but objects were not withheld from training: policies were trained separately for each object, and state policies used motion capture. Runs permitted manual resets after drops or sticking. These results establish substantial specialist performance under the reported conditions, rather than novel-object generalization or a continuous intervention-free session.

The same study included downstream demonstrations such as screwing in a lightbulb. Those demonstrations used scripted arm motions and in-hand goals, so they provide evidence of useful task integration without establishing general autonomous tool use or deformable-object handling. Both October studies are arXiv reports; the supplied materials do not establish peer-reviewed publication or independent replication.

DeepMind's July 30, 2026 Gemini Robotics 2 blog includes a caption acknowledging that multi-finger dexterous manipulation remains challenging. This is a dated laboratory assessment, not a comprehensive survey of all systems. The review retained full text for the blog and both arXiv papers, with no reported extraction truncation, but did not visually inspect their figures or videos or the blog's numerical chart bars. The reported findings above rest on textual evidence. Because the supplied search record is empty, these sources establish dated progress through October 27, 2026, rather than exhaustive coverage of the field as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: one robot completes three task families in one continuous autonomous session using objects withheld from training: in-hand reorientation and regrasping of rigid objects; use of an ordinary hand tool, such as a fastener driver or cutter; and manipulation of cloth or a bag. Evaluation should include multiple objects and task instances within each family. This is a proposed operational test of ROB-02, not an established community standard.
completion_criteria.label: One continuous autonomous session completes three withheld-object task families

completion_criteria.text: Proposed human comparison: skilled people perform the same goals on the same objects under explicitly matched conditions. Before testing, define the object coverage, repetitions, session duration, success conditions and acceptable differences from human performance. Report success, completion time and drops for every task family and for the full session, together with all interventions and resets. Reporting these metrics without predefined acceptance conditions would leave the phrase human reliability insufficiently specified.
completion_criteria.label: Skilled humans matched under predefined conditions with complete outcome reports

completion_criteria.text: Proposed autonomy and reliability accounting: distinguish successful autonomous recovery from a failure followed by human assistance, and retain all attempts in the results. Teleoperation may support development and debugging, but teleoperated evaluation does not meet the autonomy requirement. Long sessions should expose degradation and repeated failure modes rather than consist only of selected successful clips. These proposed checks respond to the reviewed study's emphasis on sustained reliability, drops and robustness, but their exact implementation and thresholds remain to be chosen.
completion_criteria.label: Long-session logs separate autonomous recovery from teleoperation and human assistance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make the task definitions, training exclusions, hardware configuration, sensing requirements, evaluation procedure and complete outcome records available for independent repetition. State the demonstrated object sizes, materials, wrist orientations, disturbances and environmental conditions. Report whether external tracking or other specialized infrastructure is necessary, and evaluate any claim of safe work near people separately. These disclosures would define where the result is practically usable.
completion_criteria.label: Records enabling independent repetition and stating practical operating boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Optional stronger demonstration: transfer the same architecture across multiple hands with different geometries or actuation arrangements, documenting what retraining or adaptation is required. Success on a finite set of hands and objects establishes demonstrated breadth within that set. It cannot prove applicability to every possible hand or object, and cross-hand transfer is not required to meet ROB-02.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Differing-hand transfer of one architecture with adaptation needs documented

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — ROB-01, “Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments,” overlaps with ROB-02 when general physical work requires finger dexterity. The dimensions remain distinct: a generalist using a simple gripper may complete many tasks, while a highly dexterous specialist may operate only at one workstation. The supplied roster gives only ROB-01's title, so its precise boundary cannot be established here.

Roster-based synthesis — ROB-03, “An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot,” concerns actuation technology that might enable better hands; ROB-02 concerns the resulting manipulation capability and does not require artificial muscles. ROB-07, “Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation,” could contribute models and planning methods for finger contacts, but useful contact prediction alone would not demonstrate ROB-02's integrated autonomy, breadth or reliability.

Roster-based synthesis — ROB-09, “Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills,” could help a dexterous robot accumulate and combine manipulation skills. ROB-02 could nevertheless be demonstrated with a fixed trained system, while lifelong learning could be demonstrated on physical skills that do not require dexterous fingers. Learning over time and dependable hand performance are related but separate achievements.

Roster-based synthesis — ROB-04, “Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock,” and ROB-08, “Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material,” may benefit from dexterous assembly or tool use. Their defining outcomes concern reproduction and collective construction, respectively. Neither follows from a dexterous hand, and their titles do not establish that human-like finger manipulation is necessary.

Roster-based synthesis — ROB-05, “Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines,” concerns changing machine structure. Such matter might form manipulators, but structural reconfiguration is distinct from controlling ordinary tools and objects with sustained human-comparable reliability.

Roster-based synthesis — ROB-06, “Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body,” and ROB-10, “Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients,” share demands for precise physical interaction. Their defining requirements concern access, medical intervention and complete clinical procedures. ROB-02 does not establish those outcomes, and specialized medical manipulation need not demonstrate broad dexterity with everyday tools and deformables.

change_log.reason: Dataset size is not an autonomous real-world success count, and the supplied review does not establish independent reproduction.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether any system outside the reviewed sources meets the full ROB-02 target as of November 1, 2026.
The Billard and Kragic structured abstract and its attributed wording remain unverified because no source artifact was retained.
Independent replication and peer-reviewed publication of the October 2026 arXiv results are not established by the supplied materials.
The exact precise-success tolerance underlying the reported 75.6% result is not specified in the supplied review and has not been inferred.
Human-performance acceptance margins, object coverage, repetitions, session duration and allowed infrastructure remain to be defined for the proposed completion test.
The historical provenance of the phrase universal dexterous manipulation principle remains unresolved.
ROB-01's precise scope and the detailed dependencies among roster concepts cannot be determined from titles alone.

brief.title: Robot hands with dependable human-level skill
possible: A robot could handle unfamiliar objects, use ordinary hand tools and work with cloth or bags in the same sustained session. It could shift an object within its fingers and change its grip as the task develops, at a speed and reliability comparable to a person.
why: This would expand the physical work robots can do in places built around human hands. Maintenance, trades, food preparation and garment work could gain machines that keep a useful grip through changing tasks, with dependable performance across repeated attempts.

sources.showed: Google DeepMind demonstrated knot tying and sealing a resealable bag with a robot hand. It also demonstrated tasks with grippers, which hold objects between opposing fingers.
sources.quote:
It can also operate standard two-fingered parallel grippers on a
Franka Duo platform
to perform complex dexterous tasks (e.g. tight packing).
sources.cited_for: Robot hands can already perform selected delicate tasks.
sources.not_established: These demonstrations do not establish sustained human-level performance across unfamiliar objects, tools and cloth.

sources.showed: This is a review of trends and challenges in robot manipulation.
sources.cited_for: It provides historical context for the difficulty of robot hand skills.
sources.not_established: A review does not demonstrate a robot meeting the combined target.

sources.showed: Their preprint presents DexSuite, software for simulated robot manipulation, with 4,700 successful simulated episodes generated by people, scripts and learned controllers.
sources.quote:
We present DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework for
dexterous manipulation built on the Genesis simulator.
sources.cited_for: Shared simulation tools support training and comparison of robot hand skills.
sources.not_established: Successful simulated episodes do not establish autonomous human-level performance on physical robots.

sources.showed: Their preprint reports 95.2% success moving objects within a LEAP robot hand under a loose accuracy test. Controllers were trained for each object; this result used external motion tracking, and trials allowed manual resets.
sources.quote: Our robot hand reaches diverse in-hand object poses at any wrist orientation.
sources.cited_for: A specialist robot hand can reach varied object positions and orientations within its grasp.
sources.not_established: This does not establish learning-independent handling of unfamiliar objects or continuous operation without human help.

shown: Chuang and colleagues also demonstrated screwing in a lightbulb, using scripted arm movements and targets for the fingers. This connects a specialist hand skill to a useful task, but leaves general autonomous tool use unproven.
missing: A combined demonstration must handle unfamiliar rigid objects, ordinary tools and cloth or bags in sustained autonomous operation.
The same system must match skilled people in speed and reliability under agreed testing conditions.
Long sessions must demonstrate recovery from slipping, drops and sticking without human assistance.

milestones.label: A continuous session succeeds across unfamiliar objects and tasks
milestones.explanation: A robot would have to adjust and regrasp rigid objects, use an ordinary tool and handle cloth or a bag in a continuous session with objects excluded from training. This would establish the combined skill.

milestones.label: Performance matches skilled people under agreed conditions
milestones.explanation: Matched trials would have to meet predefined human-performance criteria and report success, time, drops and all assistance across tasks and the full session. This would give human-level reliability a clear meaning.

milestones.label: Long sessions distinguish autonomous recovery from human help
milestones.explanation: Complete results would have to retain every attempt and distinguish the robot's own recovery from human control or assistance. This would expose repeated failures and declining performance.

milestones.label: Independent repetition establishes practical operating boundaries
milestones.explanation: Shared methods and complete results would have to support independent repetition and define hardware, sensing and operating limits, with safety near people assessed separately. This would establish where the capability works.

milestones.label: Optional transfer succeeds across different robot hands
milestones.explanation: The same control design would have to work across hands with different shapes or mechanisms, with adaptation needs documented. This would establish broader usefulness beyond the required capability.

uncertain: Human-performance margins, test duration, object coverage and permitted supporting equipment remain to be defined.
The preprint results have not yet been established through independent replication.
Finger coordination, sensing errors and physical limits of the hand may each constrain dependable performance.

page.title: Human-level dexterous manipulation
page.definition: One robot uses tools and manipulates unfamiliar rigid and deformable objects with a skilled person's precision, speed and reliability. In-hand manipulation changes an object's position or orientation relative to the palm through finger movements.

goal.need: Manual work requires accurate placement and repeated success. A LEAP-hand preprint submitted on 27 October 2026 tested 1,200 goals across four separately trained objects and six wrist orientations. Success fell when pose tolerances tightened. This evaluation does not establish integrated handling of unfamiliar objects, tools and deformables.

figures.caption: LEAP-hand goal-reaching success under two pose tolerances.
figures.note: Unfiltered state policy using motion capture. Orientation measures axis tilt for the lightbulb and wineglass. These preprint results are not peer reviewed.

statements.quote: We are continuing to advance the level of precision and speed to achieve human-level dexterity.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology
statements.quote: Human-like perception and dexterity have been identified as critical capabilities for the future of robotics

completion.title: A robot reaches OECD manipulation level 5, matching skilled-human manipulation.
completion.criterion: The robot meets OECD level 5: it independently generalises to novel objects, tasks and changing conditions; rapidly repositions objects in-hand; handles slippery and flexible materials; places objects within tight tolerances; and performs fastening and force-based operations. Under strict time constraints, precision, efficiency, robustness and adaptability equal a skilled human's, including human collaboration and refusal of tasks beyond capability.
completion.set_by: OECD AI and Future of Skills project, OECD AI Capability Indicators Technical Report, chapter 11.
completion.threshold_quote: Robots at this peak level can match human abilities in terms of manipulation tasks.
completion.basis: OECD's highest manipulation level covers the combined capability. It gives a qualitative criterion without a task battery, equivalence margin or session duration.

milestones.title: A robot hand completes all six pick-and-place tasks in the New Dexterity Test.
milestones.criterion: The robot completes MT01, MT03, MT05, MT07, MT09 and MT11, each with four objects sequentially: it grasps randomly posed cylinders or cuboids, orients their engraved faces upward and places them in designated holes. Every task in the category must succeed to earn its star. Validation used ten people and palm-mounted grippers; those gripper trials do not demonstrate autonomous control.
milestones.set_by: University of Auckland New Dexterity Research Group, published test protocol, sections 3.2, 4.1 and 4.4.
milestones.threshold_quote: A robot gripper is awarded one star on successful completion of all the tasks in a given task category.

milestones.title: A robot hand reaches an unseen in-hand goal within 2 cm and 0.4 rad in 10 s.
milestones.criterion: An unseen goal pose is reached within both tolerances at any instant in its 10 s window, without a hold requirement. Chuang and colleagues' LEAP-hand protocol allows manual resets after drops or sticking and tests new poses of trained objects.
milestones.set_by: Chuang and colleagues, real-robot evaluation protocol, Appendix J; specified for a LEAP hand and four trained objects.
milestones.threshold_quote: The coarse tolerance is 2 cm and 0.4 rad, the precise one 1 cm and 0.2 rad

milestones.title: A robot infers an unknown object's grasping properties and uses them to manipulate and place it.
milestones.criterion: The robot meets euRobotics manipulation ability level 8: it picks up an unknown object, determines its generic grasping properties, and uses them to determine how to manipulate and place it. Categorising the object is optional. This qualitative definition specifies no success percentage or speed.
milestones.set_by: euRobotics, Robotics 2020 Multi-Annual Roadmap, section 3.6.1.3, level 8.
milestones.threshold_quote: The robot is able to pick up an unknown object and determine the generic grasping properties of that object.

milestones.title: A robot manipulates rigid and deformable objects under stringent time constraints.
milestones.criterion: The robot meets OECD level 4: it handles rigid, articulated and deformable objects amid clutter, occlusion and confined spaces; reorients, places and fastens accurately; performs force-based surfacing with moderate adaptation; generalises moderately; and meets stringent time constraints. Human confirmation may remain necessary. Google DeepMind reported knot tying and sealing a ziplock bag on 30 July 2026, without establishing this complete level; these developer results are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: OECD AI and Future of Skills project, chapter 11, level 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: Approaching human efficiency with respect to time constraints

not_found: Searches of OECD, NIST, euRobotics and DARPA documents found no end-to-end test specifying human-equivalence margins and an intervention-free session duration.
Billard and Kragic's Science review could not be opened through its DOI.

results.finding: Apollo 2 with a SharpaWave hand performed 2 deformable-object tasks; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The reported tasks were tying knots and sealing a ziplock bag. The source does not establish the full OECD level 4 capabilities or stringent time constraints.
results.quote: The model can now control the five-fingered, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand on the Apollo 2 robot to complete delicate actions like tying knots or sealing a ziplock bag.

results.finding: A simulated dexterous hand achieved 50% success on Drill to Point across 150 evaluation episodes.
results.detail: The tool-use result bears on manipulation capability, but the experiments do not establish OECD level 4, including deformable-object handling, generalisation and stringent time constraints.
results.quote:
State-based diffusion reaches 50%
onDrill to Point, with 48% of diagnostic rollouts failing
at final alignment.

results.finding: The unfiltered LEAP hand state policy reached 95.2% of 1,200 unseen goals within the coarse tolerances.
results.detail: Goals concerned four objects with separately trained policies. Each had a 10-second window; success required reaching both tolerances at any instant. Drops or sticking prompted manual resets.
results.quote:
Without the filter,
the state policy reaches 95.2 % of all goals at the coarse
success tolerance

results.finding: The LEAP hand screwed in a lightbulb until it lit in 4 of 5 unfiltered trials.
results.detail: The arm motions and in-hand goals were hard-coded. The result demonstrates a fastening task but does not establish the full OECD level 4 requirements, including deformable-object handling and stringent time constraints.
results.quote:
The wineglass task succeeds in 7 of 10
trials without the filter and 6 of 10 with it, the lightbulb lights
up in 4 of 5 and 3 of 5, and the duck ends upright in 7 of 10
and 3 of 10.

results.finding: Robot succeeded in 43 of 64 unseen-object trials across manipulation tasks, including property-guided rearrangement.
results.detail: In rearrangement, the robot used tactile-inferred rigidity and contents to select grasping and placement strategies. Exploration used predefined procedures in a separate phase. The 43/64 result aggregates all evaluated tasks; rearrangement success on unseen objects was 67%.
results.quote:
For downstream manipulation, conditioning policies on
tactile-derived semantic context improves target selection
and property-dependent manipulation, raising task success from 41% to 92%
on seen objects and from 19% to 67% on unseen objects
compared with policies without object context.

results.finding: RL-100 folded boxes in a mean 41.4 seconds across 50 successful episodes.
results.detail: The task-specific policies span multiple robot embodiments. The results do not establish the complete OECD level 4 criterion, including fastening and force-based surfacing amid clutter, occlusion and confined spaces.
results.quote:
DP -2D 
requires 65.1s, while RL-100 (CM) completes in 41.4s (1.57× faster) and RL-100 (DDIM) in 45.6s, 
demonstrating that RL fine-tuning plus one-step distillation yields tangible deployment-time gains 
on long-horizon tasks.
